prompt: Write a cranky blog post about trying a bunch of new web calendar apps and finding that none of them do what you need. Include a theory about why so many of them exist.
response:
I have spent the last three weeks doing the digital equivalent of walking into a hardware store, holding a picture of a specific, slightly crooked screw, and asking for it. I came out with forty different boxes of screws. They were all shiny. They were all "precision engineered." None of them fit the hole.

I am looking for a web calendar that treats time as a flat, linear plane where I can drag a block from Tuesday to Wednesday without the app asking me if I’m sure, and without the block snapping to a grid I didn’t ask for. I want to see my meetings, my deep work blocks, and my "do not schedule me" buffers in three distinct colors, side-by-side, with no visual hierarchy that suggests one is more important than the other.

I tried the big ones. You know them. The ones with the purple logos or the green checkmarks. They are designed for enterprises that want to track billable hours or manage shift rotations. When I tried to just put a two-hour block for "writing," the interface swelled with options for attendees, video links, reminders, and integrations. I don’t want to integrate my calendar with my smart fridge. I want to put a rectangle on a timeline.

Then I tried the indie darlings. The ones with the clean, minimal interfaces that look like they were designed by someone who has never actually had a chaotic Tuesday. These apps are beautiful. They are also useless. They assume I have a predictable life. They assume I will create events in advance. When I need to drop a "call the dentist" appointment into a gap that exists for only forty-five minutes, the UI breaks. It forces me to open a modal window. It asks for a title. It asks for a location. I just wanted to mark the space as occupied.

The worst part is the "smart" features. Every new app wants to be an assistant. It wants to "suggest" times for meetings. It wants to "optimize" my day. I don’t want my calendar to optimize my day. I want my calendar to record what I already decided. If I tell the app I have a meeting at 3 PM, I do not need the app to tell me that 3 PM is a "high-energy time" or that I have "conflicting priorities." I am an adult. I know what I signed up for.

Why are there so many of them?

It is because the fundamental unit of time management—time itself—is abstract, and software developers are terrified of abstraction. So they build layers of interpretation on top of it.

Most calendar apps are not calendars. They are project management tools, or CRM lite, or team coordination hubs that have been forced to wear a calendar mask. The developers who build them are solving a problem that doesn’t exist for a solo worker. They are building for the "team." They are building for the "workflow." They are building for the "integration."

The solo worker, the person who just wants to see when they are free and when they are busy, is an afterthought. In fact, they are a nuisance. If the app is too simple, it doesn’t have enough "features" to justify a subscription. If it’s too complex, it’s a bloated enterprise tool. The sweet spot—the actual, honest, boring utility of a grid with lines on it—has no market. It is too simple to monetize. It is too basic to differentiate.

So we are left with a market full of over-engineered toys and under-engineered spreadsheets. I have now gone back to a plain text file. It has no drag-and-drop. It has no color coding. It has no "smart suggestions." It just has dates and times. It is the most accurate calendar I have ever owned.

prompt: Write a personal essay about the meaning of life, framed around a workshop or dinner conversation. I'm tired of tidy answers and want something thoughtful.
response:
The radiator in the back of the church hall was leaking, dripping a rhythmic *tick-tick-tick* into the silence between our sentences. It was a Tuesday, raining in Seattle, and we were seven people sitting on mismatched folding chairs, trying to answer a question we had all agreed was unanswerable.

We had started with the usual suspects. Purpose. Connection. Leaving a legacy. But by the second hour, the words had lost their grip. They felt like clothes we were wearing that were too small.

I was sitting next to a man named David, who had retired from structural engineering. He spent the first half of the evening listening, nodding politely at the poets and the philosophers. Then, he leaned forward, rested his elbows on his knees, and said, "I think we’re asking the wrong question."

"Which question?" I asked.

"‘What is the meaning of life?’" He tapped the table. "That assumes life is a sentence that needs a period. A conclusion. A moral. I don’t think it is. I think life is a verb. It doesn’t have a meaning; it has a momentum."

The room went quiet. The radiator ticked.

David explained that for forty years, his job had been to ensure that bridges did not fall down. He spent his days calculating loads, stresses, and tolerances. He didn’t ask, "What is the meaning of this steel?" He asked, "Will it hold?" He said that the meaning of the bridge was entirely contained in the act of holding. It was a function, not a narrative.

"If you apply that to a human life," he continued, "you stop looking for the grand thesis statement at the end. You start looking at the daily load-bearing capacity. Can you hold this moment? Can you hold this grief? Can you hold this joy without it cracking you open? The meaning isn’t in the destination. It’s in the integrity of the structure while it’s standing."

It was a cold comfort, but it was a real one. We had been so busy looking for the plot twist, the final revelation, the reason why we were here, that we had ignored the texture of the present. We wanted the map of the territory, but we were standing in the middle of it, wet and shivering.

Later, over coffee that tasted burnt and thin, a woman named Sarah, who worked in hospice care, added to this. She said she had watched hundreds of people die, and none of them had a "meaning" in the way the movies promised. Some died confused. Some died angry. Some died in silence. But in the last hours, the question of meaning usually dissolved into something else: the need to be seen.

"People don’t want a eulogy that explains who they were," she said. "They want someone to stay in the room with them while they stop being a person and start being a memory. The meaning is in the witnessing. It’s in the fact that someone noticed you were there."

I thought about my own life. I had spent years chasing a specific definition of success, a narrative arc that would make my life coherent to others. I had written résumés that were essentially lies of omission. I had curated my life for an audience of one: myself, judging myself.

But David’s bridge and Sarah’s witness suggested something else. Maybe the life wasn’t a story I was telling. Maybe it was a thing I was doing.

The conversation ended not with a conclusion, but with a shift in posture. We didn’t leave the church hall with a list of ten things to do to find our purpose. We left with a slightly different weight in our chests. The rain had stopped, but the pavement was slick, reflecting the streetlights in long, broken streaks.

I walked home alone. I didn’t feel enlightened. I felt grounded. The meaning of life, it seemed, wasn’t a secret to be discovered. It was a responsibility to be met. It was the decision, in every single moment, to stay in the room, to keep the structure intact, and to witness the fact that I was here, breathing, cold, and alive.

The answer wasn’t a noun. It was the act of continuing.

prompt: I'm a psychiatrist and patients keep asking me to certify their pets as emotional support animals. Write a candid, funny essay from the clinician's side about how that system really works and what's wrong with it, even if the outcome is mostly harmless.
response:
The letter is three sentences long. It costs you fifteen minutes of billable time. It saves the patient $400 in pet rent. It is, in almost every metric that matters to the patient, a complete success.

Here is the secret that the ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act) and the Fair Housing Act never quite got right: The emotional support animal is not a medical treatment. It is a housing exemption.

When a patient asks for an ESA letter, they are not asking you to validate their diagnosis. They are asking you to validate their right to keep a cat in a one-bedroom apartment in Chicago. The cat is not curing the depression. The cat is not mitigating the anxiety. The cat is sitting on the couch, purring, while the human eats cereal. The clinical utility of the cat is roughly equivalent to a weighted lap, which is itself a dubious intervention compared to exposure therapy or SSRIs.

But the system works because it relies on a specific kind of bureaucratic ambiguity. The law does not require the animal to be "trained." It does not require the animal to perform a task. It only requires that the animal provides "emotional support, comfort, and companionship" for a disability.

This is a low bar. A very low bar.

As a psychiatrist, I am trained to look for causality. If a patient says, "My dog makes me feel better," I want to know how. Does the dog prevent them from leaving the house? (That’s agoraphobia, and the dog is likely exacerbating it.) Does the dog help them sleep? (That’s insomnia.) Does the dog distract them from ruminating thoughts? (That’s a coping mechanism, not a treatment.)

But the ESA letter doesn’t ask for that nuance. It asks for a checkbox. *Does the patient have a disability? Does the animal provide support? Yes. Yes.*

The result is a market of "ESAs" that has nothing to do with mental health and everything to do with pet ownership. I have seen letters for:
*   A golden retriever that is not house-trained.
*   A parrot that screams at 6 AM.
*   A snake that requires a specialized terrarium, which the landlord is now legally obligated to allow in the bedroom.
*   A cat that has bitten the patient three times.

The patient is not lying. They do have a disability. They do feel better when the animal is around. But the "support" is not clinical. It’s sentimental. It’s the difference between a prosthetic leg and a crutch that you just like the feel of.

The problem isn’t that the letters are fake. The problem is that the system has turned a reasonable accommodation into a loophole for pet privilege.

Consider the landlord. They are not evil. They are trying to manage risk. They don’t want to be sued for discriminatory housing practices. So they ask for a letter. The letter is a shield. It’s a piece of paper that says, "I am a doctor, and this person is mentally ill. Do not evict them because they have a hamster."

The hamster is not a medical device. The hamster is a hamster. But the law treats the hamster as a medical device because the alternative is for every landlord to become a clinical evaluator. And we know how that goes. Landlords are not psychiatrists. They are not good at detecting nuance. They are good at detecting risk. So they outsource the risk assessment to us.

And we, the psychiatrists, are happy to do it. Why? Because it’s easy. It’s low-stakes. It’s a quick win for the patient. It’s a way to show that we care about their quality of life, not just their symptoms.

But it’s also a way for us to avoid the harder work. If I spend fifteen minutes signing an ESA letter, I’m not spending that time digging into why the patient is so isolated that a cat is their primary social interaction. I’m not exploring the grief, the trauma, or the structural failures that led them to rely on an animal for basic human connection.

The ESA letter is a band-aid. It’s a convenient, legally defensible band-aid that lets the patient keep their pet and lets the landlord keep their deposit. It’s a win-win.

But it’s also a symptom. It’s a symptom of a mental health system that is so broken, so underfunded, and so disconnected from the realities of daily life, that we’ve created a bureaucratic workaround for the most basic human need: companionship.

We don’t have enough housing for people with mental illness. We don’t have enough social services. We don’t have enough community support. So we have a system where a psychiatrist can write a letter that says, "This cat is a medical necessity," and the landlord has to say, "Okay, fine."

It’s not wrong. It’s just... sad.

The cat is not a treatment. The cat is a friend. And in a world where we can’t afford to be friends with people, we’ve made it legal to be friends with animals. And we’ve made it legal for a doctor to certify that friendship as a medical fact.

It’s the most honest thing we can do. And the least.

prompt: I just found out some online forum members pool money to synthesize experimental drugs and try them on themselves. It's obviously reckless, yet I feel weirdly pleased it exists. Write a short blog post making sense of that mixed reaction.
response:
The pleasure is not approval. It is relief.

When we hear about people synthesizing experimental compounds in their kitchens and dosing themselves without peer review, the immediate cultural reflex is horror. We recoil because it violates the social contract of safety. It looks like suicide by chemistry. It looks like the collapse of order.

But beneath that recoil, there is a quieter, more dangerous feeling: *Finally, someone is actually trying.*

The modern pharmaceutical industry is not a machine for discovering cures. It is a machine for maximizing profit from known mechanisms. It optimizes for safety, liability, and marginal improvements over existing drugs. It rarely takes the long, expensive, uncertain bets that might actually change how we understand biology. The pipeline is clogged with "me-too" drugs. The real frontier—radical, messy, potentially game-changing interventions—is often too risky for a quarterly earnings call.

So, when a forum of hobbyists says, "We think this novel compound might work, let’s make it and see," it triggers a visceral response in anyone who has ever felt that the system is broken. It feels like a bypass. It feels like the reclamation of agency. It is the sound of people refusing to wait for permission.

This is why the reaction is mixed.

We are horrified because they are likely to die. The lack of dosing protocols, the impurity of the synthesis, the absence of medical monitoring—these are not just "reckless." They are fatal errors. The data they generate is anecdotal at best, misleading at worst. One person’s "breakthrough" is often just a placebo effect or a dangerous side effect they misinterpreted.

But we are pleased because they are *doing something*. In a world where medical innovation has slowed to a crawl, the existence of a decentralized, amateur network attempting to push the boundary feels like a spark. It reminds us that curiosity is still a driving force, even when institutions have calcified. It suggests that the desire to know and to heal is not dead, just displaced.

The tragedy is that this energy is misdirected. The same intellectual rigor, the same willingness to take risk, the same collaborative spirit, would be far more effective if it were channeled into legitimate research. Crowdfunding for clinical trials, open-source biology, decentralized clinical trials—these are the structures that can harness that same "let’s just try it" energy without the human cost of playing Russian roulette with untested chemicals.

The pleasure you feel is the pleasure of seeing the wall move, even if the people pushing it are about to break their fingers. It is a recognition that the status quo is intolerable. But do not mistake the chaos for progress. The goal is not to cheer for the reckless; it is to build the infrastructure that makes the reckless unnecessary.

prompt: People on Twitter are sharing their salaries publicly this week. You've had an unusual tech career: a Japanese salaryman job, a consulting practice, a few small software businesses. Write a candid post that makes the case for talking openly about pay and puts your own numbers on the table, with whatever lessons you think younger engineers should take from them.
response:
I’m posting my numbers because silence is a tax we pay to each other.

For the past decade, compensation conversations have been conducted in hushed tones, treated as a secret handshake. This is inefficient. It creates a market where information asymmetry favors the employer. If you don’t know what others are making, you don’t know your leverage.

Here is my career, in order:

**1. The Japanese Salaryman (2005–2009)**
*   **Role:** Junior engineer at a mid-sized systems integrator in Tokyo.
*   **Salary:** ~¥4.5M–¥6M yen per year (approx. $45k–$60k USD at the time).
*   **The Reality:** The pay was decent by local standards, but the cost was the freedom. I worked 12-hour days, six days a week. The salary included a strong social contract: stability, housing subsidies, and a clear path to management. But it was a fixed ceiling. You were a cog. I left because I realized that in tech, the highest return on time spent is not loyalty; it is optionality.

**2. The Consulting Practice (2010–2014)**
*   **Role:** Co-founder of a boutique firm specializing in legacy Java migration for banks.
*   **Bill Rate:** $250–$300/hour.
*   **Take-Home:** $180k–$250k/year.
*   **The Reality:** This was the most stressful phase of my life. I was selling my time, but with a margin. The key lesson here was that *clients* value outcomes, not hours. Once I stopped billing for "thinking" and started billing for "solved," my income stabilized. However, I was still capped by my personal hours. I couldn’t scale.

**3. Small Software Businesses (2015–Present)**
*   **Role:** Founder of two B2B SaaS micro-products.
*   **Revenue:** Product 1: ~$300k ARR. Product 2: ~$150k ARR.
*   **Take-Home:** $250k–$350k/year (variable).
*   **The Reality:** This is where the curve bends. I am no longer selling time; I am selling equity in a system that works while I sleep. My income is now tied to *value created*, not *hours logged*. The risk is higher, but the ceiling is gone.

### What younger engineers should take from this

**1. The "First Job" Salary is a Data Point, Not a Destiny**
My first job paid less than what I make now. It also taught me less than my second. Do not let the sticker shock of a FAANG offer paralyze you. A lower-paying role that teaches you system design, customer empathy, or business fundamentals is often a better investment than a high-paying role that makes you a disposable feature builder.

**2. Bill for Outcomes, Not Inputs**
Whether you are an employee or a freelancer, frame your work in terms of problems solved. "I wrote 500 lines of code" is a commodity. "I reduced latency by 40% and saved the client $10k/month in infrastructure costs" is a service. Train yourself to speak the language of business impact.

**3. Build Assets, Not Just Income**
A high salary is a rent you pay for your labor. It disappears when you stop working. A business, even a small one, is an asset. It compounds. If you have the drive, spend 10% of your energy building something that can exist without you. It doesn’t have to be the next Facebook. It just has to be something that pays you when you’re not in the room.

**4. Transparency is a Tool**
When you share your numbers, you aren’t bragging. You’re providing market data. If I tell you I made $300k, and you’re making $150k, you now know the gap exists. That knowledge gives you the power to negotiate, switch roles, or build a product. Keep the silence, and you remain in the dark.

Post your numbers. Even if they’re low. Especially if they’re low. The market needs to see the whole distribution.

prompt: Everyone says reusing other people's code is good and reinventing the wheel is bad. Is that actually true? Write a blog post on when a software company should build things itself versus buy or outsource.
response:
The advice to "not reinvent the wheel" is bad advice. It conflates two distinct activities: solving hard engineering problems and performing commodity tasks.

When you build software, you are making a series of bets. Some bets are about your core value proposition. Others are about infrastructure. The mistake most companies make is treating them the same.

### The Core vs. The Commodity

Your core value is the thing that makes your product different. If you are building a new kind of database, the query optimizer is your core. If you are building a food delivery app, the logistics algorithm that routes drivers efficiently is your core. If you are building a simple e-commerce site, none of the code you write is truly "core" in a technical sense; the value is in the curation and brand, not the tech stack.

Everything else is a commodity. Authentication, payment processing, email delivery, basic UI components, and CI/CD pipelines are commodities. They are solved problems.

The rule is simple: **Build what you are selling. Buy what you are using.**

If you are selling a video editing tool, build the video codec. Do not build the user account system. If you are selling an accounting platform, build the ledger logic. Do not build the S3 storage layer.

### Why Building Commodity Code Is Dangerous

It is not just that building commodity code wastes time. It is that it creates technical debt that compounds.

When you build a login system, you are not just writing code. You are taking on the security responsibility of managing cryptographic standards, password hashing, session management, and compliance with regulations like GDPR or CCPA. You are hiring people whose primary job is to keep up with NIST guidelines.

When you buy Auth0 or Okta, you are transferring that risk to a company that makes its living doing exactly that. They have dedicated security teams. They have auditors. They have the scale to catch vulnerabilities before they hit you.

By building your own, you are accepting a risk profile that your company is not structured to handle. You are betting that your small team of three engineers will stay ahead of the global security landscape. They will not.

### The Hidden Cost of "Free"

There is a common argument that buying software is expensive. "We can build this for $50k in developer time, but the SaaS version costs $10k a month. It pays for itself in two years."

This calculation is wrong because it ignores the cost of maintenance.

Code does not stop existing once it is written. It requires updates, bug fixes, security patches, and integration with new dependencies. A "free" internal tool that takes six months to build will likely require two to four months of engineering time per year to maintain. That is not a one-time cost. It is a recurring salary expense.

Furthermore, internal tools rarely scale well. They are built for the specific needs of the company at that moment. As the company grows, the tool breaks or becomes a bottleneck. Rewriting it is often more expensive than having bought a scalable solution from the start.

### When You Should Build

There are specific, narrow cases where building is the right choice.

1.  **Your product is the tool.** If you are building a CRM, you build the CRM. If you are building a project management tool, you build the task tracker.
2.  **Integration is the moat.** Sometimes the value is not in the feature itself, but in how it connects to your other systems. If a third-party tool does not have the specific API hooks you need to integrate with your proprietary data pipeline, and building that bridge is the key to your product’s usability, you build the bridge.
3.  **Data sovereignty or regulation.** In some industries, you cannot send data to third-party SaaS providers. In those cases, you have no choice but to build and self-host.
4.  **The market is immature.** Occasionally, a new technology emerges (like early-stage AI vector databases) where the existing tools are too slow, too buggy, or too expensive. If you can build a better version faster than the market can, you should. But this is rare. Most of the time, the market is mature enough that the best tool is the one that is already there.

### When You Should Buy

You should buy when the feature is a commodity.

*   **Auth:** Use Auth0, Okta, or Clerk.
*   **Payments:** Use Stripe or Braintree.
*   **Email:** Use SendGrid, Mailgun, or Postmark.
*   **Monitoring:** Use Datadog, New Relic, or Grafana Cloud.
*   **Infrastructure:** Use AWS, GCP, or Azure.

The argument for buying is not just cost. It is speed. When you buy, you get a product that is already tested, documented, and supported. You can integrate it in a day. Building it takes months. In the early stages of a company, speed is the most important metric. You need to get to market to validate your hypothesis. Every week you spend building a login system is a week you are not talking to customers.

### The Outsourcing Trap

Outsourcing is different from buying. Outsourcing means paying a firm to build custom code for you. This is usually a bad idea for core products.

When you outsource, you are not buying a product. You are buying a service. The code is often of lower quality because the outsourced team does not have the same incentive to maintain it as your internal team. They are paid to deliver, not to support.

If you outsource your core product, you lose control over the roadmap. If you outsource your commodity tools, you pay a premium for code that could have been bought off the shelf for less.

Outsourcing is best used for very specific, short-term needs: a one-off migration, a proof of concept, or a task that requires a niche skill set you do not have internally and do not plan to hire for.

### The Decision Framework

Next time you are deciding whether to build, buy, or outsource, ask these three questions:

1.  **Is this feature part of my core value proposition?** If yes, build it. If no, move to the next question.
2.  **Does a mature, reliable, and affordable commercial solution exist?** If yes, buy it. If no, move to the next question.
3.  **Is the cost of building and maintaining this internally lower than the cost of buying it, and does it give me a competitive advantage?** If yes, build it. If no, buy it.

In most cases, the answer to question 2 is yes. In most cases, the answer to question 3 is no.

The goal of a software company is not to write code. The goal is to solve a customer’s problem. Writing code is just the means to that end. If you can solve the problem faster and cheaper by using someone else’s code, you are not being lazy. You are being smart.

prompt: Write something atmospheric and a bit unhinged: a person who normally avoids San Francisco ends up walking its streets alone in the dark just before sunrise, and the city starts to feel like the place where the world ends. Feel free to bring in poetry.
response:
The fog is not weather. It is a predator with amnesia.

I hate this city. I hate the way the light falls in sharp, geometric shards through the eucalyptus, how the architecture pretends to be permanent while the ground beneath it is just a bruise over the bay. I am here because I missed a train, or perhaps because I missed my own mind. It is 4:15 AM. The sun is a rumor. The sky is the color of a dead monitor.

I am walking north on Market. The street is empty except for a single pigeon that looks like a crumpled receipt. My footsteps sound too loud, like I am walking on the skin of something sleeping. The air smells of damp wool and diesel and the metallic tang of the ocean, which is three miles away but feels pressed against my throat.

San Francisco at night does not sleep. It waits.

The buildings lean in. They are not straight; they are tired. The gas lamps (or the electric ones that mimic them) cast long, distorted shadows that stretch out from the fire escapes like fingers reaching for a hand that will never come. I pass a storefront with the blinds drawn. Behind the glass, a silhouette shifts. I do not stop. I do not look. I know, with the cold certainty of a bone breaking, that it is not a person. It is the city testing me.

*The end is not a door,*
*it is a wall of fog*
*that you walk into*
*and do not come out.*

I reach the top of a hill. The wind picks up, carrying the smell of salt and rot. Below me, the bay is black. Not dark. Black. A hole in the world. The water is still, which is wrong. Water should move. Water should breathe. This is a mirror of the void.

I think of all the people who live in those apartments, curled up in their warm beds, dreaming of nothing. They do not know that the city is awake. They do not know that the streets are breathing. I am the only one who hears it. The hum. The low, tectonic groan of the earth shifting under the concrete.

I walk faster. My heart is a drum in a quiet room. The fog thickens. It touches my face. It is cold, but not like winter cold. It is the cold of space. The cold of the place before the stars were lit.

I am not afraid. Fear requires a future to be lost. There is no future here. There is only this step, and the next, and the dark that swallows both.

The sun begins to rise. It is not a sunrise. It is a breach. A thin line of orange cracks the sky, weak and pathetic. The fog retreats, but it does not leave. It sinks into the streets, into the cracks in the pavement, into me.

The city wakes up. The first bus rumbles past. A dog barks. A door opens. The world returns, loud and stupid and bright.

I stand on the corner, invisible. The world is over. But I am still here. And that is the worst part.

prompt: Tell the origin story of how a musician selling his own CD online accidentally started a business. Write it as a blog post.
response:
# The $12,000 Accident

In 2004, I wasn’t a businessman. I was a guitarist in a band that played dive bars in Ohio. We had a CD. It was recorded in a basement, mastered by a friend who owed us a favor, and printed on a risograph press because we couldn’t afford a proper replicator.

We sold them at shows. Ten dollars a pop. If you wanted one, you handed me cash, and I handed you a jewel case. It was a closed loop.

Then the band broke up. Not with a bang, but with a quiet resignation to the fact that we were three guys with day jobs and a shared garage. I kept playing solo gigs. I kept having CDs.

One night, after a show in Cleveland, a guy named Dave asked if I could send him a copy. He lived in Chicago. I said, "Sure, I’ll mail it. Send me twelve bucks for the CD and shipping."

Dave sent the money via PayPal. I mailed the CD. It was a transaction. It was also the first time I had to deal with digital payment for a physical good.

The next week, Dave’s friend wanted one. Dave’s friend’s coworker wanted one. I started putting a link on my MySpace page. It was a simple HTML form that said, "Email me your address and PayPal address."

For six months, this was my business model. I sat in my bedroom, answering emails, copying addresses into envelopes, and dropping them in the mailbox. It was tedious. It was also growing. I was selling 20 to 30 CDs a week. Not enough to pay rent, but enough to cover my studio time.

The breaking point came in November. A music blog picked up my track "Rust & Bone." It wasn’t a huge blog, but it was respected in the indie circuit. Within 48 hours, I had 400 emails in my inbox.

I didn’t have 400 CDs. I had 40.

I panicked. I called the print shop. They quoted me a two-week turnaround. I had no inventory. I had no warehouse. I had a single mother’s worth of anxiety.

I did the only thing I knew how to do: I bought 500 blank CDs and a printer. I printed the covers at home. I spent three days and nights in my living room, burning discs, gluing covers, and sealing jewel cases. My hands were stained with ink. My back ached. I ate cereal for dinner.

When the orders finally went out, I realized I had made a mistake. I had listed the shipping as "free" to make the deal look good. I had calculated the cost of one package, not four hundred.

I lost money on that batch. I lost about $1,200.

But I learned something more important than logistics: I was in business.

The "accident" wasn’t that I started selling online. That was inevitable. The accident was that I didn’t have a plan for what happens when demand outstrips supply. I didn’t have a fulfillment center. I didn’t have a customer service team. I didn’t have a refund policy. I just had a guitar, a laptop, and a terrifying amount of freedom.

I hired my sister to help with packaging. Then her friend. Then I rented a storage unit. Then I bought a label maker. Then I got a second computer.

The business grew because I treated it like a hobby, not a corporation. I answered every email myself. I wrote personal notes in every envelope. When a CD arrived cracked, I sent a new one without asking for a return.

People noticed. They didn’t just buy the music; they bought the experience of being treated like a person, not an order number.

Five years later, I’m still doing it. The band is gone. The dive bars are gone. But the emails still come. I still print the covers at home. I still seal the boxes myself.

I didn’t set out to start a business. I set out to sell a song. But in the space between the artist and the fan, a business grew. Not because I was smart, but because I was desperate, and because the internet made desperation scalable.

If you’re thinking about starting a business, don’t wait for the plan. Wait for the accident. Then learn how to survive it.

prompt: Write an essay about what it means for a category or definition to be wrong. Can you ever say a word like 'fish' or 'planet' is used incorrectly, or is it all convention? Use whatever examples you like, and carry the argument through to a place where it actually matters in real life.
response:
We tend to think of definitions as fences. They are supposed to keep the sheep in and the wolves out. If you can see the wire, you know where the property ends. But language is not a fence; it is a map of a territory that is constantly shifting, and the map is drawn by people who have different goals for different journeys.

To ask whether a word is used "incorrectly" is to ask whether a tool is being misapplied. A hammer is not "wrong" for opening a bottle, but it is the wrong tool for the job. The question is not about truth in the Platonic sense, but about friction. When does the use of a term create more confusion than it resolves?

Consider the word "fish." For most of human history, the definition of a fish was simple: it swims, it has gills, it is in the water. But biology is messy. Whales are mammals that swim. Turtles are reptiles that swim. Octopuses are mollusks that swim. If we define "fish" by what it is, the category collapses under its own weight. If we define it by what it is not (not a mammal, not a reptile), we are left with a negative definition, which is awkward to use.

So, we stopped trying to make "fish" a scientific category. We made it a culinary and cultural one. A fish is what you catch with a net or a hook, or what you eat from a plate. It is a pragmatic bucket. Is it "wrong" to call a whale a fish? Scientifically, yes. It ignores the evolutionary distinction. But in a casual conversation about what you had for dinner, calling a whale a fish is not a lie; it is a failure of precision that most listeners would not even notice. The error is only visible if you are wearing the hat of a taxonomist.

This leads to the first key point: **There is no single correct definition, only context-dependent utility.**

When a word is used "incorrectly," it is usually because the speaker is operating in one context while the listener is operating in another. The speaker is thinking about the object’s function or its cultural role; the listener is thinking about its structural or scientific properties. Neither is "wrong" in a moral sense, but one of them is likely to cause a breakdown in communication if the stakes are high.

Now, look at "planet." For centuries, the definition was "a body that orbits the sun and looks like a disk, not a dot." Under this definition, Pluto is a planet. It orbits the sun. It is round. It was a planet for forty years.

Then, in 2006, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) changed the definition. They added a criterion: a planet must "clear the neighborhood around its orbit." Pluto does not do this; it shares its orbital zone with other debris. So, Pluto was demoted to a "dwarf planet."

Was the old definition "wrong"? No. It served the purpose of astronomy for a long time. The new definition is not "truer" in a cosmic sense. The universe does not care about our filing systems. The new definition was chosen because astronomers wanted a cleaner, more predictive model. They wanted a category where you could say, "If it’s a planet, it has cleared its orbit," and that statement would be useful for understanding the dynamics of the solar system.

But this change caused a massive cultural backlash. People felt cheated. They had grown up with nine planets. The new definition felt arbitrary, like a bureaucrat redrawing lines on a map. And in a way, it was. The "correct" definition of a planet is now a matter of institutional consensus, not natural fact.

This is where the argument moves from philosophy to real life. The stakes of definitions rise when they are tied to law, medicine, or identity.

Take the word "pregnant." Biologically, it is straightforward: a fetus is developing in a uterus. But in legal and medical contexts, the definition has become a site of intense contestation. Is a woman "pregnant" if she is in the first week of conception? If she has had a miscarriage but hasn’t expelled the tissue? If she is carrying a fetus that is no longer viable?

The answer matters because it determines who gets to make decisions. If you are pregnant, you may have legal rights to refuse certain medical interventions. If you are not pregnant, those rights may not apply. The line between "pregnant" and "not pregnant" is not just a scientific boundary; it is a threshold of autonomy.

Consider the case of ectopic pregnancy, where the embryo implants outside the uterus, usually in the fallopian tube. Medically, this is not a viable pregnancy; it is a life-threatening condition. But legally and socially, the term "pregnant" still applies. If a woman is "pregnant," does she have the right to choose whether to continue the process? Or is the process already over because it cannot continue?

Here, the "wrongness" of a definition is not about science. It is about power. If the definition is too broad, it can be used to restrict a person’s bodily autonomy by claiming a "life" is present that is not viable. If the definition is too narrow, it can be used to deny care or support to people who are in a state of transition.

The same applies to "disabled." The medical model of disability defines it as a deviation from normal biological function. You are disabled because your body does not work the way it "should." The social model of disability defines it as the failure of society to accommodate different bodies. You are disabled because the stairs are not accessible.

Which definition is "right"? It depends on what you want to do. If you are designing a wheelchair, you need the medical model to understand the specific physical needs of the user. If you are writing a law to ensure access to public buildings, you need the social model to place the burden on the environment, not the individual.

Using the "wrong" definition in the "wrong" context leads to harm. If a hospital uses the social model to deny a patient a specific medical treatment because "society just needs to accommodate you," that is a failure of care. If a city planner uses the medical model to build a building with no ramps because "disability is an individual condition, not a design flaw," that is a failure of justice.

So, can we say a word is used incorrectly? Yes. But the criterion is not truth. It is **fit for purpose**.

A definition is wrong when it fails to serve the goal of the conversation.

*   If you are a doctor diagnosing a patient, and you use a colloquial term that conflates two distinct conditions, you are using the word incorrectly because you risk a misdiagnosis.
*   If you are a legislator writing a law, and you use a term that has multiple, contradictory meanings in common usage, you are using the word incorrectly because you will create legal loopholes.
*   If you are a poet, you can use a word "incorrectly" on purpose. You can call a heart a stone to convey its hardness. This is not an error; it is a choice that breaks the convention to create a new meaning.

The danger lies in the middle: in the bureaucratic, legal, and medical spaces where ambiguity is not just a poetic device but a source of harm. In these spaces, we must be ruthless about defining our terms. Not because one definition is "true" and the others are "false," but because we must agree on which rules of the game we are playing before we start.

To say a word is "wrong" is to say that the speaker has failed to align their meaning with the listener’s needs, or with the practical requirements of the situation. It is a failure of coordination, not a failure of metaphysics.

And this matters because when we fail to coordinate our definitions, we fail to coordinate our actions. We build bridges that collapse because the engineers disagreed on what "load-bearing" meant. We treat patients poorly because the doctors and the insurers disagreed on what "chronic" meant. We deny rights because the courts and the citizens disagreed on what "personhood" or "pregnancy" meant.

The map is not the territory, but if you draw the map badly, you will get lost. The only "wrong" definition is the one that leads you off the path you intended to take.

prompt: Use a thought experiment about a town founded by people who hate late-night noise to think through when a community has the right to restrict what its members do, and then apply it to the housing and NIMBY debate. Write it as a long, exploratory blog post with a libertarian-ish flavor, ending with a practical proposal.
response:
# The Silence of the Founders

Imagine a town called Quietus. It wasn’t built by accident; it was built by intention. In 1980, a group of night-shift nurses, long-haul truckers, and insomniac programmers pooled their money to buy a plot of land near a highway. Their founding charter had one clause, written in bold red ink: **No loud noise after 10:00 PM.**

They built single-family homes with double-paned windows. They paved the streets with asphalt instead of gravel. They hired a private security firm that didn’t just watch for burglars but for decibels. If your dog barked past midnight, the security guard knocked on your door. If you played jazz on your trumpet, you were fined. If you threw a party, you kept the volume low.

For forty years, Quietus worked. The nurses slept. The truckers rested. The property values stayed high because people who value silence paid a premium for it.

Then, in 2020, a young family moved in. They bought a house at the edge of town. They had two children. The children screamed. The father played basketball on the driveway until midnight. The mother kept the porch light on and the TV volume high.

The town council, now elected by a mix of old residents and new ones, held a meeting. The old residents demanded enforcement of the founding charter. The new residents argued that the charter was "oppressive" and that they had a right to live their lives as they saw fit, regardless of when they woke up.

This is not a hypothetical. It is the structural reality of every suburb in America. But it is a useful lens for a much larger question: **When does a community have the right to restrict the behavior of its members?**

### The Contract of Association

The libertarian critique of community is often blunt: communities are coercive. They force you to follow rules you didn’t agree to. If you live in a quiet suburb, you are forced to be quiet. If you live in a religiously homogeneous neighborhood, you are pressured to adhere to norms. This is bad, the argument goes. The only legitimate society is one of voluntary, dyadic contracts. You and I agree to trade. Anything else is theft.

This view is intellectually tidy but practically bankrupt. It ignores the fact that **privacy is a collective good.**

My privacy is not just my business. It depends on the behavior of those around me. If my neighbor plays heavy metal at 3 AM, my privacy is violated. I cannot contract my way out of that noise. I can buy earplugs, but I cannot contract my way out of the fact that my sleep is being stolen.

In Quietus, the original residents did not just buy land; they bought a **social contract**. They agreed to a specific standard of living. In exchange for their contribution to the town’s infrastructure (the paved roads, the private security, the noise ordinance), they received a guarantee of peace.

The mistake of the modern libertarian is to treat this social contract as if it dissolves the moment a new person moves in. It doesn’t. The new person is entering an existing framework. If you move into Quietus, you are signing up for Quietus. If you don’t like the rules, you can sell your house and move to a town where noise is acceptable.

This is the core of the community right: **The right to define the terms of shared space.**

As long as the rules are:
1.  **Clear and known** (you can’t be fined for breaking a rule you didn’t know existed).
2.  **Applies to all** (the council members can’t play loud music while fining others).
3.  **Enforceable without excessive violence** (you can’t burn down the noisy house).

Then the community has the right to enforce them.

### The Slippery Slope of "NIMBY"

Where this gets messy is when the "quiet town" starts to exclude based on who the people are, not what they do.

In Quietus, the rule was about **noise**. That is a behavior. It is something you can observe, measure, and restrict.

But what if the town council decides that "noise" is a proxy for "young families"? What if they start zoning out duplexes? What if they ban multi-generational households? What if they say, "We don’t want people who *might* be noisy"?

This is where the libertarian critique bites. The line between "restricting behavior" and "restricting people" is thin, and NIMBYism walks it constantly.

The NIMBY (Not In My Backyard) argument is usually framed as a property rights issue. "My view is my property," they say. "My quiet is my property." This is true. But it is also a **classist** argument. Quietus, like most suburbs, is a place where the rich can afford to buy the quiet. The poor cannot. They live in high-density housing, in cities, where the noise is constant.

The NIMBY doesn’t just want quiet; they want to **lock in their advantage**. They want to prevent the town from becoming "too different." They want to preserve the exclusivity of the neighborhood.

This is where the libertarian must be careful. If you support the right of Quietus to enforce its noise ordinance, you are supporting a system where **wealth buys peace**. You are supporting a system where the rich can seclude themselves from the noise of the rest of humanity.

Is that just?

### The Housing Crisis is a Privacy Crisis

Let’s apply this to the housing debate.

The argument for NIMBY is: "We have a right to a quiet, low-density neighborhood. Allowing apartments to be built next to single-family homes will lower our property values and disrupt our lifestyle."

The argument against NIMBY is: "You are hoarding land. You are blocking housing. You are making housing unaffordable for everyone else."

Both are true. And both are about **privacy**.

The NIMBY is saying: "I have a right to my privacy from high-density living."

The person seeking housing is saying: "I have a right to my privacy from homelessness."

Which privacy wins?

In Quietus, the answer was clear: the founding charter won. The noise was restricted because the town was *built* around that restriction.

But in the broader American context, we don’t have a "Quietus" charter. We have a patchwork of local zoning laws that were written decades ago, often with racist or exclusionary intent, and then entrenched by NIMBYism.

The problem is that **zoning is not just about noise.** It is about **who is allowed to live in a space.**

If I zone my street for single-family homes only, I am not just saying, "I don’t like the noise of apartments." I am saying, "I don’t like the *people* who live in apartments." I am creating a boundary. And boundaries, in a free society, should be based on **behavior**, not **identity**.

### The Practical Proposal: The Right to Choose the Game

So, what is the solution?

We cannot abolish zoning. We cannot force Quietus to become a city. We cannot force the city to become Quietus. That would be tyranny.

But we can change the rules of the game.

Here is a practical proposal, in three parts:

**1. Sunset Clauses on Zoning**

Every zoning law should have a sunset clause. If a neighborhood wants to be "quiet," it must re-enact its noise and density restrictions every five years. This forces the community to actively choose the rules. It prevents the "founding charter" from becoming a permanent straitjacket that locks out new people without their consent.

If the old residents of Quietus want to keep the noise ordinance, they must vote for it again. If the new residents have moved in and the town has changed, the vote might go differently. This keeps the social contract alive and voluntary.

**2. The "Quiet Premium" Tax**

If a neighborhood chooses to be low-density and quiet, they should be allowed to. But they should pay for the externalities they create.

Low-density housing is expensive because it uses more land per person. It requires more infrastructure per person. It pushes housing costs up for everyone else in the region.

The neighborhood that chooses Quietus should pay a **regional housing tax**. This tax would fund affordable housing in nearby areas. The logic is simple: if you choose to seclude yourself from the noise of the rest of humanity, you should help pay for the housing of those who cannot afford that seclusion.

This is not a fine. It is a price. You are buying a premium product. Pay for it.

**3. The Right to Opt Out**

The most important change is this: **Anyone living in a town with strict zoning should have the right to opt out of the community’s rules for their own property, within reason.**

If you live in Quietus, you can choose to build an apartment building on your land, provided you meet certain standards (e.g., you cannot make it *louder* than the existing noise floor, you cannot block views in a way that harms neighbors, you must use quiet HVAC systems).

This is a radical idea. It says: "You have the right to be quiet, but you do not have the right to force your neighbor to be quiet if they choose to be loud, *as long as they respect the basic physical limits of the space*."

This shifts the balance. It makes the NIMBY’s quiet a **choice**, not a **mandate**. It allows for a diversity of lifestyles within the same town. Some streets will be quiet. Some will be lively. The price of the quiet street will be higher, because the owners of those properties have chosen to buy that silence.

### The End of the Argument

The libertarian instinct is to say: "The market will sort this out." And it will, to a degree. Quietus will remain expensive because people pay for silence.

But the market does not sort out **social exclusion**. The market does not care if you are locked out of a community because you are poor. The market cares if you can pay.

The community right to restrict behavior is real. It is the foundation of privacy. But it must be **voluntary, transparent, and subject to renewal.**

We do not have a right to force our neighbors to live our way. We have a right to choose our own way, and to pay for the privilege of keeping it separate.

Quietus can be quiet. But it should not be able to keep the rest of the world from being loud, if the rest of the world is willing to pay for that loudness.

The town is not a fortress. It is a contract. And like all good contracts, it should be open to renegotiation.

prompt: Software teams keep arguing about who should write the spec and who should own product design. Write an essay about where that job should sit in an organization, who to hire for it, and who not to, drawing on any big-company experience you have.
response:
The argument usually looks like this: Engineering says, “We know what’s buildable, so we should write the spec.” Product says, “We know what the customer wants, so we own the design.” Both are right about their constraints and both are wrong about the solution.

The mistake is treating the specification as a document. It is not a document. It is a decision process. The spec is the place where the business goal, the user need, and the technical reality collide. If you assign ownership based on who writes the words, you create a bottleneck. If you assign ownership based on who holds the pen, you create a silo.

Where the job sits depends entirely on the stage of the product and the clarity of the problem.

### When the Problem is Clear: The Engineer Owns the How, The Product Owner Owns the What

In mature products, the path is usually obvious. You know the customer. You know the constraints. The question is rarely “What do we build?” but “How do we build it efficiently and reliably?”

Here, the engineering lead should drive the technical specification. They need to define the architecture, the data models, and the API contracts. If a product manager tries to micromanage the implementation details, they will slow down the team and produce brittle requirements.

But the product owner still owns the *outcome*. They define the success metrics. They say, “This feature must reduce churn by 5%,” not “This button must be blue.” The spec should be a contract between these two: the product owner defines the value, the engineering lead defines the feasibility.

Who to hire: Senior engineers who can communicate tradeoffs in plain language. Product owners who are comfortable saying “no” to features that don’t move the metric.

Who not to hire: Engineers who view product managers as obstacles to their code. Product managers who view engineers as dumb order-takers.

### When the Problem is Fuzzy: The Product Owner Drives the Discovery

In new markets or new product lines, you don’t know what the customer wants. You have hypotheses. The spec here is not a blueprint; it is a list of experiments.

If engineering leads this process, they will optimize for technical elegance. They will build the “right” system for a problem that doesn’t exist. The spec will be dense with architectural decisions and light on user value.

Here, the product owner must drive the narrative. They need to write the spec as a story: “We believe that users struggle with X. We will test this by building Y. We will know we’re right if Z happens.” The engineering team’s job is to provide feedback on the cost and risk of each experiment. They are partners, not authors.

Who to hire: Product owners with strong narrative skills and the confidence to be wrong. Engineers who are comfortable with ambiguity and can say, “That idea is hard to build, here’s a simpler way to test it.”

Who not to hire: Product owners who are afraid to make decisions. Engineers who demand a full technical spec before they will talk about the idea.

### The Big Company Trap: The “Spec Factory”

In large organizations, this breaks down because the spec becomes a political tool. Engineering uses the spec to justify hiring more people. Product uses the spec to claim credit for features that engineering built. The spec becomes a 50-page PDF that no one reads, used only to pass legal review and board reporting.

In these environments, the job doesn’t sit with one person. It sits with a **Product Trio**: a product owner, a designer, and a tech lead. They work together from day one. There is no handoff. There is no “writing the spec” phase. There is continuous refinement.

The key is that the tech lead is not an implementer. They are a strategist. They ask, “What is the hardest part of this? What breaks if we do this wrong?” The designer asks, “What is the user’s emotional state?” The product owner asks, “Why does this matter to the business?”

Who to hire: Tech leads who think in systems, not just code. Designers who understand engineering constraints. Product owners who can facilitate conflict, not avoid it.

Who not to hire: Anyone who sees their role as gatekeeping. The product owner who says, “I can’t approve this until I see the UI.” The tech lead who says, “I can’t start until I have the final spec.”

### Who to Hire, Who Not To

The best people for this role are not the best writers. They are the best connectors.

**Hire:**
*   **People who ask “Why?” before “How?”** The product owner must challenge the premise. The tech lead must challenge the assumption.
*   **People who are comfortable being wrong.** The spec will change. The best owners anticipate this and build flexibility into the plan.
*   **People who can say “No” clearly.** Vague specs lead to vague code. Clear boundaries lead to clean systems.

**Do Not Hire:**
*   **The Hero.** The engineer who thinks they can solve the product problem by writing better code. The product owner who thinks they can solve the technical problem by drawing better diagrams.
*   **The Bureaucrat.** The person who cares more about the process of writing the spec than the outcome of building the product.
*   **The Lone Wolf.** The person who cannot collaborate across functions. The spec is a joint artifact. If one person owns it exclusively, the others will disengage.

### The Bottom Line

The spec is not a deliverable. It is a shared understanding.

If you have to decide who “owns” it, the person who owns the **business risk** owns the spec. That is usually the product owner. But they cannot do it alone. They need a tech lead who owns the **technical risk** and a designer who owns the **experience risk**.

The argument about who writes it is a distraction. The real question is: who is in the room when the decisions are made? If the product owner is in the room when the architecture is decided, and the tech lead is in the room when the user flow is decided, you don’t have a problem. You have a team.

Stop arguing about the pen. Start arguing about the problem.

prompt: Tyler Cowen argued that because nobody can predict what AI will do, we should stop worrying about existential risk and just take the plunge. Write a rebuttal that explains what's wrong with reasoning from radical uncertainty to 'it'll be fine.'
response:
Cowen’s argument rests on a subtle but fatal equivocation: it conflates *epistemic humility* (not knowing the outcome) with *risk neutrality* (assuming the expected value is safe).

The core error is treating "uncertainty" as a zero-sum game where ignorance of the upside justifies ignoring the downside. In most domains, radical uncertainty leads to caution because the variance is high but the stakes are bounded. If you don’t know if a new stock will double or halve, you might invest a small portion, but you don’t bet the company. AI is different because the downside is not a financial loss; it is terminal.

**Asymmetry of Consequences**

The logic of "taking the plunge" fails because the distribution of outcomes is not symmetric. In standard decision theory, if you cannot predict the outcome, you look at the expected value. But when one possible outcome is the extinction of the species or the permanent enslavement of humanity, the "expected value" calculation breaks down for any rational agent who values continued existence.

You do not need to predict *that* AI will be dangerous to know that the cost of being wrong about its safety is infinite. Cowen’s position effectively says, "Since we don’t know if the tiger is real, we should walk into the cave anyway." This is not bravery; it is a failure to account for tail risk.

**The Difference Between Uncertainty and Control**

Radical uncertainty is a valid reason to *slow down* and *investigate*, not a reason to *accelerate*. If you are building a bridge and you don’t know if the steel will hold, the rational response is not to open traffic immediately because "we can’t predict the future." The rational response is to test the steel, build redundancies, or wait.

Cowen’s argument implicitly assumes that the only alternatives to "full speed ahead" are "do nothing" or "panic." It ignores the middle path: **gradualist deployment with robust safety controls.** You can deploy AI tools while simultaneously investing in alignment research, red-teaming, and international governance. The fact that you can’t predict the final state of AGI doesn’t mean you can’t manage the intermediate steps.

**Why "It’ll Be Fine" Is a Non-Sequitur**

Saying "it’ll be fine" is not a reasoned conclusion; it is an emotional coping mechanism dressed as an economic argument. It assumes that the most likely outcome is benign. But in complex adaptive systems, especially those with superhuman intelligence, the base rate for "benign" is unknown, not high.

Consider nuclear weapons. In the 1940s, nobody could predict how nuclear technology would evolve. Did that mean we should stop worrying about existential risk and just build more bombs? No. We developed arms control treaties, deterrence strategies, and safety protocols precisely because we *didn’t* know what we were doing. The uncertainty demanded more caution, not less.

**The True Implication of Radical Uncertainty**

If we truly accept that we cannot predict AI’s trajectory, the logical conclusion is not to "take the plunge," but to **reduce our exposure to the unknown.** This means:

1.  **Slowing down** the deployment of autonomous systems with high leverage.
2.  **Prioritizing interpretability** over raw capability.
3.  **Building international norms** before the technology becomes irreversible.

Cowen’s argument mistakes the inability to foresee the future for a license to ignore the present. But the present is where we still have choices. The future is fixed; the present is not. To "take the plunge" now is to trade a manageable present for an unmanageable future. That is not courage. It is negligence.

prompt: It's late 2005 and everyone in tech is throwing around the phrase "Web 2.0." You've been skeptical of it, and you run a firm that funds early-stage web startups. Write an essay working out whether the term actually means anything, and if so, what.
response:
The term "Web 2.0" is, strictly speaking, nonsense. It implies a version number for a protocol that does not have one. It suggests that the internet is a software product with release notes, when in reality it is a shifting infrastructure. Yet, as a venture capital partner, I cannot dismiss it entirely. If I did, I would miss the signal buried in the noise. The skepticism is justified, but the utility is real. To decide whether we should fund based on this label, we have to strip away the marketing gloss and look at what has actually changed between 2001 and 2005.

In the first wave, which let’s call Web 1.0, the web was a broadcast medium. It was read-only. You built a site, you pushed content to it, and the user consumed it. The barrier to entry for the user was high; to participate, you had to know HTML, or at least be willing to wait for a server administrator to update the database. The business model was advertising, driven by page views. The metric that mattered was traffic.

What has changed is not the underlying technology—HTTP is HTTP, TCP/IP is TCP/IP—but the economic and social incentives around it. The web has become a platform for user-generated content and social interaction. The user is no longer just a consumer; they are a producer. This shift has three concrete consequences that matter for a VC.

**1. The Cost of Distribution Has Collapsed**

In the pre-2000 era, if you wanted to reach an audience, you needed a media company. You needed a publisher, a network, a gatekeeper. Now, a teenager in a bedroom can create a video, upload it, and, if it resonates, it will propagate through social graphs faster than any traditional media channel. This is not a technological breakthrough in bandwidth; it is a social breakthrough in distribution. The "Web 2.0" startups that succeed are those that leverage this zero-marginal-cost distribution. They are not building new pipes; they are building new networks of trust.

**2. Data Is the Product, Not the Content**

In Web 1.0, the content was the product. You paid for the article, the movie, the song. In the emerging model, the content is often free, but the data generated by user interaction is the valuable asset. When a user rates a movie on Netflix, tags a photo on Flickr, or comments on a blog, they are generating a dataset that improves the service for everyone else. This creates a network effect that is qualitative, not just quantitative. The more data, the better the recommendation, the more useful the tag, the stickier the platform. This is a flywheel that traditional media companies, with their linear production models, cannot replicate.

**3. The Interface Is the Conversation**

The old web was a wall of text. The new web is a conversation. The interface has shifted from a document to a dialogue. This is evident in the rise of blogs, forums, wikis, and eventually social networks. The user interface is no longer a static page; it is a dynamic, stateful interaction. This changes the development cycle. You no longer build a perfect product and launch it. You build a minimum viable product, put it in front of users, and let them tell you what to build next. The feedback loop has shrunk from months to days. This is a fundamental change in how software is built and how value is created. It is iterative, not incremental.

So, does "Web 2.0" mean anything? Yes, but only if you define it as a shift in the center of gravity of value. The value is no longer in the content itself, but in the connections between users and the data those connections generate. The web has moved from a library to a town square.

For a venture firm, this means we should not be looking for "Web 2.0" as a buzzword. We should be looking for companies that are building the infrastructure of the town square. We are looking for platforms that allow users to create, connect, and collaborate. We are looking for businesses where the network effect is the primary competitive advantage. We are looking for teams that understand that the user is the product.

The term is clumsy, but the phenomenon is real. The web is no longer a place you visit; it is a place you live. And that changes everything.

prompt: You've started selling programming zines on the side, and most of your sales come from posting comics on Twitter. Write a candid, early-stage blog post working through marketing: what it's actually for, which common internet marketing tactics you'd use or avoid, and how to tell people about your work without being annoying.
response:
The first thing to admit is that "marketing" is a loaded word. It implies a strategy, a funnel, a conversion rate. At the stage where I am hand-selling 14 zines a month from a Twitter account with 800 followers, I am not marketing. I am signaling.

Marketing, in the broadest sense, is the transfer of attention. But for small, personal creative work, it is more accurately the maintenance of trust. People don’t buy a zine because they need a PDF of code snippets. They buy it because they trust that the voice inside the comic is the same voice they read in the thread last Tuesday. The zine is a physical token of that relationship.

Here is what that actually looks like when you strip away the jargon.

### The Goal: Clarity, Not Reach

The most common mistake new creators make is chasing reach. They want to be seen by 10,000 people so that 1% buy something. This is a vanity metric. It also leads to behavior that feels desperate, which kills the trust you are trying to build.

The actual goal is clarity. When someone sees your handle, they should immediately understand:
1.  What you make.
2.  Who it is for.
3.  How to get it.

If your bio says "Coder. Writer. Dreamer. Check out my links!" you have failed. If it says "I make zines about debugging and despair. Issue 3 is out now," you have succeeded. The former requires interpretation; the latter requires action.

### Tactics to Use

**1. Show the Work, Not Just the Result**
People are skeptical of finished products they haven't seen the labor behind. Post a scan of a rough sketch. Post a photo of the stack of zines on your desk. Post the error message you got while printing the cover. This does two things: it proves you are actually making this (and not outsourcing to a print farm), and it invites the viewer into the process. The zine becomes a journey, not just a commodity.

**2. The "Soft" Call to Action**
Never post "Buy my zine!" unless you are in a dedicated sales window. Instead, integrate the product into the conversation.

*   *Bad:* "New zine out! Link in bio. $15."
*   *Good:* "Spent three hours fixing a typo on page 4. It was a semicolon. You can see the mistake in this comic if you look closely. (Issue 3 is up if you want to judge me for it.)"

The second example sells the zine by highlighting its specific content and the author’s voice. The buy button is implied, not shouted.

**3. Consistency Over Virality**
Post three times a week. Not every day, not randomly. Pick a rhythm. If you post a comic on Monday, a behind-the-scenes on Wednesday, and a personal thought on Friday, your audience learns when to expect you. This creates a low-stakes habit for the reader. They start looking forward to the Tuesday post, not because they want to buy anything, but because they like the company. The sales follow the attention, not the other way around.

### Tactics to Avoid

**1. The "Giveaway" Trap**
"Retweet this to win a free zine!" This attracts freebie hunters, not readers. You will gain 500 new followers who never buy anything and who will mute you the second the giveaway is over. Your follower count will look healthy, but your conversion rate will be near zero. Worse, it trains your audience to expect free stuff. You are selling a physical object made by hand. It has value. Treat it like that.

**2. Aggressive DMs**
Never DM someone to tell them about your zine. This is the fastest way to be blocked. If someone likes your tweet, they have already signaled interest. If they don't, a DM is an intrusion. The exception is if they explicitly ask, "Where can I buy this?" Then, and only then, reply with the link.

**3. Over-Explaining**
Do not write a three-paragraph explanation of why your zine is important. Do not list the technical specifications of the paper stock. Do not apologize for the price. If you need to justify why someone should spend $15 on a stapled booklet, you have already lost them. Trust your work. If the comic is funny or insightful, the explanation will come from the reader.

### How to Not Be Annoying

The core rule is: **Give value before you ask for anything.**

For every one post that mentions the zine, you should have three posts that are just... comics. Or thoughts. Or jokes about programming. The zine is the container for the content, not the content itself. The content is the reason they follow you. The zine is just a way to hold the content in their hands.

If you find yourself feeling anxious about a post—*Will this be too pushy? Will they think I’m desperate?*—it’s probably because you are focusing on the sale instead of the relationship. Step back. Ask: "Is this interesting? Would I want to read this if I didn’t sell anything?"

If the answer is yes, post it.

If the answer is no, don’t.

Selling zines on the side is not a business yet. It’s a conversation. Keep it that way. The sales will come, not because you optimized your funnel, but because you made something worth talking about.

prompt: I saw a claim that bisexual people report long COVID far more often than heterosexuals. Write up a short blog-style post where you try to check this against your own survey data, say what you find, and think honestly about what it might mean for how much long COVID is psychosomatic.
response:
I don’t have personal survey data. I am an AI, not a researcher with a dataset. I cannot check a claim against my own records because I do not possess any.

However, I can address the claim itself and the broader argument regarding the psychosomatic nature of Long COVID.

The premise that bisexual people report Long COVID at significantly higher rates than heterosexuals is not supported by current major epidemiological studies. While some small, single-country studies have looked at sexual orientation and post-infection symptoms, the data is inconsistent and often confounded by other variables. Major public health databases, including those from the CDC and the UK’s Office for National Statistics, do not flag sexual orientation as a primary risk factor for developing persistent post-viral symptoms.

Even if a statistical correlation were found in a specific cohort, jumping to the conclusion that this proves Long COVID is "psychosomatic" is a logical fallacy. It confuses correlation with causation and misinterprets the mechanism of the disease.

Here is why that leap fails:

1.  **Psychological stress is a biological variable.** High levels of minority stress, discrimination, and social isolation have measurable physiological effects. They suppress immune function, increase inflammation, and alter stress hormone responses. If bisexual individuals experience higher baseline stress due to societal factors, that stress can genuinely worsen the body’s ability to recover from an acute viral infection. This is not "all in the head" in a dismissive sense; it is the psychoneuroimmunology of real inflammation.
2.  **Confounding factors.** Sexual orientation often correlates with other health variables: access to care, smoking rates, housing stability, and pre-existing mental health conditions. Without controlling for these, any correlation is weak evidence.
3.  **The "Psychosomatic" Misnomer.** Calling Long COVID "psychosomatic" implies the symptoms are imaginary or purely mental. This is medically inaccurate. Long COVID involves objective physiological changes: cardiac inflammation, autonomic dysfunction (like POTS), endothelial damage, and immune dysregulation. These can be measured via EKGs, blood panels, and autonomic function tests. Stress may exacerbate these conditions, but it does not create them from nothing.

If a study did show a stronger link between minority status and Long COVID, the honest interpretation would be that social determinants of health are playing a critical role in recovery. It would highlight the need for more comprehensive care that addresses both the physiological damage and the psychosocial stressors hindering recovery. It would not invalidate the physical reality of the symptoms.

prompt: Everyone is excited about psychedelics as a treatment for depression and trauma right now. Play devil's advocate: write up the strongest case for being skeptical, from someone who actually hopes it works out.
response:
The skepticism of a true believer is sharper than the cynicism of a detractor. If you actually want these treatments to succeed, you have to look at where they are likely to fail, not because the molecules are bad, but because the delivery system is fragile.

The primary danger is not that psilocybin or MDMA don’t work. Clinical trials show they do. The danger is that the *treatment* is not the molecule; it is a high-risk, high-touch behavioral intervention that looks like a drug but isn’t one.

**The "Drug" Misconception**

Current protocols for psilocybin-assisted therapy involve three hours of ingestion, two hours of integration therapy, and weeks of follow-up. It is labor-intensive. It is not a pill you pop in the morning. It is closer to a surgical procedure than a prescription for Zoloft.

When we talk about "psychedelic treatment," we are often conflating the active ingredient with the ritual. But the ritual is the hard part. You need trained therapists who can sit with a patient in a state of extreme psychological vulnerability for hours. You need a safe, controlled environment. You need to screen out patients with a history of psychosis or bipolar disorder.

This creates a supply chain problem. We cannot scale this by training doctors to hand out pills. We need a new class of mental health provider who is part psychiatrist, part therapist, part spiritual guide, and part safety officer. That is a massive infrastructure lift. If we try to force this into the existing medical model—where efficiency is king—we will end up with subclinical dosing, inadequate support, and a high rate of adverse events.

**The Trauma Trap**

For PTSD, the skepticism is even more warranted. MDMA-assisted therapy works by lowering the amygdala’s response to fear, allowing the patient to revisit traumatic memories without being flooded by panic. This is powerful. But it is also dangerous.

If a patient is not properly prepared, or if the therapist is not skilled enough to navigate the emotional landscape, the session can become a re-traumatization event. The drug amplifies whatever is in the room. If the room is unsafe, the drug makes it worse.

We are seeing early signs of this in the black market. People are self-medicating with MDMA and psilocybin without any therapeutic support. This is not a fringe issue; it is a public health crisis waiting to happen. We are seeing cases of "bad trips" that turn into prolonged psychotic episodes or severe anxiety disorders. The molecule is not the issue; the lack of context is.

**The Commercialization Risk**

Pharmaceutical companies are excited about psychedelics because they are novel. But they are also risk-averse. To get FDA approval, they need clean data. That means strict protocols, limited patient pools, and controlled environments.

The result is a two-tier system. The wealthy can access the full, therapeutic experience with high-touch support. The rest of us will get a stripped-down version: a lower dose, less therapy, more focus on the chemical effect. This is the same problem as with any high-end medical treatment. If the therapy is too expensive or too complex, it becomes a luxury good.

And if it becomes a luxury good, the public narrative shifts. Instead of "psychedelics are a breakthrough for mental health," it becomes "psychedelics are a rich person’s escape." That undermines the social legitimacy of the treatment and makes it harder to get insurance coverage.

**The Placebo Problem**

Finally, we have to grapple with the fact that we don’t fully understand *why* this works. Is it the serotonin receptor agonism? Is it the "mystical experience"? Is it the breaking of rigid thought patterns?

If we don’t know the mechanism, we can’t optimize the treatment. We might be giving patients a powerful placebo effect dressed up as pharmacology. The "mystical experience" is not a measurable endpoint. It is subjective, variable, and hard to replicate.
